write-ups

  • 2026-10-23 — interp / patching Agents traced a lookup pathway in Qwen3 Agents traced how Qwen3 looks up the value for a named item: three stages, each carried by a few attention heads. Six head locations found in Qwen3-0.6B were fixed in advance and tested in Qwen3-1.7B, where a separate search had found the other two stages. Interventions there moved the answer preference in the predicted direction on 92.2–100% of held-out prompts, and the transfer test passed every registered gate. Short synthetic lookup prompts in two Qwen3 sizes; preference between two candidate answers, not free generation; the 0.6B three-stage study and the repair failed their verdicts; evidence private.
  • 2026-10-23 — interp / SAEs A search for internal signals in Gemma, built and tested by agents On Gemma 3 1B, directions extracted without labels recovered parenthesis and quotation state (|AUROC| 0.78, 0.75), and one passed a preregistered steering test on fresh text: Δ 1.49 against at most 0.75 for 99 random directions from the same subspace. Gemma Scope 2 already had it, as a blend. One model; screens calibrated on parenthesis labels, with quotation as the untuned control; steering confirmed at layer 12 only; the search ran inside a Gemma Scope 2 SAE, so no new variable is certified.
  • 2026-10-18 — interp / probes What Llama’s internal signals reveal about factual accuracy On 742 held-out FActScore claims, a layer-19 probe on Llama 3.1 8B reaches AUROC 0.802, against 0.735 for P(True) and 0.740 for subject popularity, though no clear advantage over popularity is detected once whole biographies are resampled. Within biographies it keeps a signal after position controls and, in an exploratory test, adds to P(True). A preregistered decomposition attributes most of its direct signal to attention heads. One model and layer; 157 human-labelled ChatGPT biographies; the 200-neuron knockout had an effect but missed its preregistered criterion; analysis code unreleased.
    • 2026-04-25 — interp / probes · initial study Testing internal signals for factual accuracy in legal answers and biographies A linear probe on Llama 3.1 8B’s layer-19 hidden states ranks 742 held-out, human-labelled FActScore claims by correctness at AUROC 0.802, against 0.541 for Llama’s stated confidence. An exploratory legal-QA test (MAUD) shows a similar gap. The first stage of the probe project. One model and layer; FActScore claims written by ChatGPT; stronger baselines come in the follow-up; MAUD uses model-judge labels and is not yet grouped by source example.
  • 2026-10-05 — agents / formal verification Agents reused proofs of OpenSSL routines across three callers Agents verified three experimental x86-64 callers in HOL Light by applying machine-checked contracts for two unchanged Debian OpenSSL routines through their actual linkage, instead of re-deriving the routines in each caller’s proof. The held-out caller missed its three-hour cap, then completed in a separately recorded successor. Pinned x86-64 model in HOL Light; loaded image, instruction model and extraction trusted; not all of OpenSSL; replay assets unpublished; human review pending.
  • 2026-09-27 — agents / formal verification Agents turned a one-kernel Lean proof into a checker that certified 25 PyTorch kernels One Lean theorem and a small checker certified 32-bit size arguments for 25 torch.compile kernels: 15 of 35 development cases and 10 of 24 held out, each proof bound to the live compilation’s guards. Two of nine tuned kernels got faster. Inductor’s 1D pointwise kernels on one NVIDIA L4; per-lane guarantee under captured guards, with frontend and shape exporter trusted; proof checks rerunnable, timings recorded only; research prototype, not upstream.
    • 2026-09-26 — agents / formal verification · first experiment, one kernel A Lean proof let agents cut a compiled PyTorch workload’s runtime by 26% Agents declared a torch.compile kernel’s size arguments 32-bit, proved in Lean when that is exact, and cut a changing-shape workload’s runtime by 26% on one NVIDIA L4. A maintainer closed the opt-in PR unmerged and asked for issue discussion first. One program on one NVIDIA L4; the proof and patch cover one kernel class, with extraction and compiler trusted; PR closed unmerged.
  • 2026-09-25 — agents / formal verification 25 bugs in free-threaded CPython, found by agents Agents confirmed 25 bugs in CPython’s free-threaded build, 18 with no earlier report found in the tracker search. Of five reports I filed upstream, two now have fixes merged into CPython main. TLAPS and Lean proofs checked a locking model; replays of real runs showed five places CPython departs from it. One macOS arm64 machine; I have reported four of the 25 bugs and none of the 92 sweep findings so far; the proofs cover the locking model, not CPython itself.
  • 2026-09-24 — agents / formal verification · early pilot, before the PyTorch work Agents optimized four naive routines without changing their specifications Claude Opus 5.5 rewrote four deliberately naive Dafny routines while the Dafny verifier held every change to a frozen specification. Seven rewrites verified: six known algorithmic fixes and one fitted to the benchmark. On a held-out workload the run-length encoder ran 105× faster than its naive start, both measured as Dafny-compiled Python. Known algorithmic fixes to deliberately slow starts, still 5–7,400× slower than Python built-ins; one optimization run per routine on a shared machine; harness and run records unpublished.
  • 2026-05-26 — rl / sampling bias Training on random integers changes fixed-list choices across tasks Fifty GRPO steps on one pick-an-integer task moved Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct’s choices over fixed answer lists toward uniform on all nine untrained tasks (mean distance from uniform 0.74 to 0.38). On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct the shift was narrower and concentrated on integer tasks. Scores over fixed answer lists, not open-ended text; the trained model was sampled on only three tasks; small capability checks; Qwen per-task records unpublished.
  • 2026-04-24 — reasoning / tokens · exploratory A panel-format adapter produces shorter answers with lower accuracy An RL-only panel-of-experts LoRA on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base wrote far shorter completions than Qwen’s thinking model: where both were right, the thinking model’s were a median 5.9–6.9× longer. The panel was 31.5 points less accurate on matched MATH500 level-5 samples and 50.6 points on a 20-problem AIME subset. Format and training history are confounded; 20-problem AIME subset, unequal token limits, one run per training stage; tokens per correct sampled answer is a retrospective measure, not a deployment cost.
    • 2026-04-25 — rlvr / math · exploratory follow-up Exploratory follow-up on training with partially solved math problems One RL run on 354 competition problems that a panel-format Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base adapter solved on some but not all of 8 attempts raised its score on 100 held-out problems from 14% to 29% by its last evaluation (step 90 of a 100-step run). One run and seed; the held-out set was scored every 10 steps during training; no random or full-pool curriculum compared; thinking-model run not completed.
